learningObjectives.text: Explain this episode: Which journey shapes Theseus’ early exploits?
Use the cited passage to explain: Why compare these deeds with Heracles’?

main.work: Plutarch: Lives of the Noble Grecians and Romans
main.author: Plutarch
main.translator: John Dryden and others; revised by Arthur Hugh Clough
main.locator: Life of Theseus, road to Athens; local text, normalized characters 11878-12184
main.excerpt: himself of all those that should offer any. And first of all, in a set combat, he slew Periphetes, in the neighborhood of Epidaurus, who used a club for his arms, and from thence had the name of Corynetes, or the club-bearer; who seized upon him, and forbade him to go forward in his journey. Being pleased
main.note: Verbatim local text with whitespace normalized. Lesson analysis is interpretation, not part of this quotation.

narrativeBlocks.title: The scene
narrativeBlocks.body: Plutarch tells how Theseus travels to Athens by land and confronts violent figures along the road. The young hero models himself on Heracles, but his journey also prepares his recognition in Athens.

narrativeBlocks.title: What the source does
narrativeBlocks.body: Source quotation (translation; whitespace normalized): “himself of all those that should offer any. And first of all, in a set combat, he slew Periphetes, in the neighborhood of Epidaurus, who used a club for his arms, and from thence had the name of Corynetes, or the club-bearer; who seized upon him, and forbade him to go forward in his journey. Being pleased”

narrativeBlocks.title: Why it matters
narrativeBlocks.body: Interpretation: The road is a political training ground: each removed threat helps explain why a community might want this hero as a founder.

narrativeBlocks.title: Read it carefully
narrativeBlocks.body: Plutarch shapes a legendary life from inherited material. Theseus’ emulation of Heracles helps explain the young hero’s choices within that biography; it is not an eyewitness account of his journey.

narrativeBlocks.title: Carry it forward
narrativeBlocks.body: A founder myth turns heroic violence into a claim about safety and shared identity.
